topic.subject: social
topic.title: Food security in India
topic.scope: availability, access and affordability, buffer stock, public distribution system, ration shops, famine

misconceptions.statement: Food security means that every village must produce all the food it consumes.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse local self-sufficiency with national food security.
misconceptions.fix: Food security is achieved when food is available through production, imports, and efficient distribution, not just local production.

probe.question: If a region grows only cotton, is it food insecure?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it does not grow its own food.

misconceptions.root_belief: local production is the only source of supply

misconceptions.statement: If food is available in the market, everyone is food secure.
misconceptions.why: Students equate market availability with individual access.
misconceptions.fix: Access requires the ability to purchase food; even if food is available, the poor may lack the money to buy it.

probe.question: Why do people starve when shops are full of grain?
probe.wrong_answer: Because there is no food available in the country.

misconceptions.statement: Buffer stocks are kept to make profit by selling grain when prices rise.
misconceptions.why: Students apply commercial business logic to government welfare functions.
misconceptions.fix: Buffer stocks are maintained by the FCI to ensure food availability during shortages and to stabilize prices for the poor.

probe.question: Why does the government store grain?
probe.wrong_answer: To sell it at high prices later for profit.

misconceptions.root_belief: all economic activity aims for profit

misconceptions.statement: Ration shops provide free food to everyone in the country.
misconceptions.why: Students conflate the existence of a system with universal free access.
misconceptions.fix: Ration shops provide food at subsidized prices, and they are targeted primarily at families below the poverty line.

probe.question: Who can buy from a ration shop?

misconceptions.root_belief: government services are always free for all

misconceptions.statement: If India produces record foodgrains, no one in the country can be food insecure.
misconceptions.why: Students equate total production with food security and ignore distribution and purchasing power.
misconceptions.fix: Food security needs availability, access and affordability together; even with high production, poor households may not be able to buy enough food.

probe.question: India has record wheat and rice production this year. Can some people still go hungry? Explain.
probe.wrong_answer: No, because when production is high everyone gets enough food.

misconceptions.root_belief: Total production alone guarantees food security
misconceptions.source_hint: Class 9 NCERT Economics, Ch. 4 and teacher observation

misconceptions.statement: India depends mainly on imported food grains to feed its people.
misconceptions.why: Students link food shortage and food security with imports, and recall past episodes like the 1960s wheat imports.
misconceptions.fix: India is self-sufficient in foodgrains after the Green Revolution, mainly wheat and rice; it feeds its people from its own production and holds buffer stocks.

probe.question: Where does most of the grain for India's ration shops come from?
probe.wrong_answer: It is mostly imported from other countries.

misconceptions.root_belief: India still relies on foreign grain

misconceptions.statement: The poor are food insecure only because there is not enough food in the country.
misconceptions.why: Students think hunger comes from scarcity and overlook lack of income and employment.
misconceptions.fix: Poor people go hungry mainly because they lack the money to buy food (low purchasing power), even when food is available.

probe.question: Why can a poor landless labourer be hungry even when godowns are full?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the country does not have enough food.

misconceptions.root_belief: Hunger always comes from food scarcity
misconceptions.source_hint: Amartya Sen entitlement approach in NCERT discussion

misconceptions.statement: The Food Corporation of India sells ration to people directly in the villages.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse FCI with ration shops, since both are connected to PDS.
misconceptions.fix: FCI buys wheat and rice from farmers at minimum support price and stores it; ration shops (fair price shops) sell to consumers.

probe.question: Who buys wheat from farmers at MSP and who sells it to card-holders?
probe.wrong_answer: FCI does both, buying from farmers and selling to consumers at its shops.

misconceptions.root_belief: FCI and ration shops are the same body

misconceptions.statement: The government fixes minimum support price after the harvest, so it can lower it when there is a surplus.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up MSP with market price and think it changes with supply.
misconceptions.fix: MSP is announced by the government before the sowing season to encourage farmers to grow crops and ensure them a fair price.

probe.question: When is the minimum support price announced and why?
probe.wrong_answer: After harvest, to match the market price when there is a surplus.

misconceptions.root_belief: MSP is the same as market price

misconceptions.statement: Every household with a ration card gets food at the same price.
misconceptions.why: Students think the PDS is uniform and overlook the categories of cards.
misconceptions.fix: Under targeted PDS, cards are issued as Antyodaya, BPL and APL, and each category gets a different quantity at a different price; poorer families pay less.

probe.question: Does a BPL family pay the same price for ration as an APL family?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all card-holders pay the same price at the ration shop.

misconceptions.root_belief: All ration cards carry identical benefits

misconceptions.statement: A famine means many people have died of starvation, so deaths are needed to call it a famine.
misconceptions.why: Students see starvation deaths as the definition of famine, though deaths are a result.
misconceptions.fix: Famine is widespread hunger because of a lack of food or purchasing power, shown by rising food prices and people migrating; deaths are the extreme result, not the definition.

probe.question: Can a region be called famine-hit before anyone has died of starvation?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a famine only exists once many people have died.

misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Class 9 Economics Ch. 4; Bengal famine 1943 discussion

misconceptions.statement: A famine is caused only by drought or crop failure.
misconceptions.why: Students link famine with a natural disaster, forgetting that the Bengal famine of 1943 happened without a major fall in food availability.
misconceptions.fix: Famines also arise from lack of access: when people lose income or prices rise sharply, they cannot buy food even when stocks exist.

probe.question: Name the only cause of a famine such as the Bengal famine.
probe.wrong_answer: A drought that destroyed the crops.

misconceptions.root_belief: Natural disaster is the only cause of famine
misconceptions.source_hint: Amartya Sen's work on the Bengal famine; NCERT Class 9
